articles.title: China September industrial profits jump 14.4% y/y, rebounding from 4.2% in August
articles.desc: The rebound offers a modest positive surprise for Chinese assets at a time when sentiment is fragile, with onshore equities in a bear market and Morgan Stanley warning of further downside in offshore shares. Industrial and materials stocks are the most direct beneficiaries, and the data may slightly
articles.content: The rebound offers a modest positive surprise for Chinese assets at a time when sentiment is fragile, with onshore equities in a bear market and Morgan Stanley warning of further downside in offshore shares. Industrial and materials stocks are the most direct beneficiaries, and the data may slightly ease concerns about a sharp earnings slowdown. Commodity-linked currencies such as the Australian dollar could find mild support from any read-through to Chinese industrial demand. That said, the gently slowing year-to-date trend and the lack of a sector breakdown limit how far markets are likely to run with the headline. PBOC sets USD/ CNY central rate at 6.7171 (vs. estimate at 6.6731) China’s factory profits shook off August’s slump in style, though the year-to-date trend is still drifting gently lower beneath the bounce. Summary: China’s industrial profits rose 14.4% y/y in September, up from 4.2% in August Year-to-date profits rose 15.5% in January to September, down slightly from 15.7% in January to August August’s 4.2% was the slowest single-month growth since November 2025 In January to August, mining and manufacturing led gains while utilities declined High-tech and AI-related manufacturing have been strong performers this year September’s rise comes on top of a strong base, after profits jumped more than 21% in September last year Profits at China’s industrial firms rose 14.4% year on year in September, a sharp rebound from 4.2% growth in August, official data showed on Tuesday. Cumulative profits for the first nine months of the year rose 15.5%, edging down from 15.7% in the January to August period. The September reading marks a strong recovery after August’s weak result, which was the slowest single-month growth since November 2025 and had followed an 11.2% rise in July. The rebound suggests August’s slowdown was not the start of a sustained downturn in corporate earnings, although year-to-date growth has continued to drift lower, from 17.6% in the January to July period to 15.5% now. Industrial profits data, published monthly by the National Bureau of Statistics, cover larger industrial companies across mining, manufacturing and utilities. The figures are watched as a gauge of corporate health and pricing power in the world’s second-largest economy, and of firms’ capacity to invest and hire. Monthly readings can be volatile, so the year-to-date figure is often a better guide to the underlying trend. Breakdowns for September were not available at the time of writing. In the January to August period, growth was led by mining, where profits rose about 35%, and manufacturing, up about 17%, while utilities recorded a decline of around 12%. High-tech and AI-related manufacturing had been strong performers, with computers and communications equipment profits more than doubling, though subdued domestic demand weighed on profitability in some industries. The rebound comes against a difficult backdrop for Chinese markets. Onshore equities are in a bear market, and Morgan Stanley warned this week that offshore Chinese shares could fall a further 10% to 15% before reaching a valuation floor, citing a weakening economy among other pressures. Firmer industrial earnings offer some counterweight to that gloomy view, at least for the industrial sector. The details of the September release, particularly which sectors drove the rebound and whether domestic demand is improving, will determine whether the strength proves durable or whether it partly reflects the month-to-month volatility typical of this series. The rise is all the more notable because it comes on top of a strong September last year, when profits jumped more than 21%. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.content: Judge upholds ousting of GB resort’s manager | The Tribune Judge upholds ousting of GB resort’s manager THE SUPREME Court has rejected a hotel management company’s bid to regain immediate control of a top Grand Bahama resort amid its furious ongoing legal battle with the property’s owner. Justice Constance Delancy, in an October 22, 2026, verdict denying the injunction sought by Island Ventures Resort & Club (IVRC), the entity established by Old Bahama Bay condominium owners to manage the property following the Ginn project’s 2011 failure, recognised “the volatility” of the battle for control and its impact on the “surrounding community”. Old Bahama Bay is a major employer and economic activity centre for Grand Bahama’s West End, but the judge ruled she was “not persuaded” that ousting the corporate owner of the resort’s properties, LRA-OBB Ltd, in favour of IVRC reclaiming management control was the best action to take. Justice Delancy’s verdict thus preserves the status quo established on August 4, 2026, when a security team and other agents acting for LRA-OBB, which stands for Lubert Adler-Old Bahama Bay, finally succeeded in repossessing the resort and seizing control from IVRC after three earlier attempts in the previous 16 months were thwarted. Lubert Adler was Ginn’s financing partner. However, IVRC is likely to draw comfort from several of the conclusions and factual findings made by Justice Delancy in her injunction ruling. These include that it has “a contractual relationship” with “some” Old Bahama Bay condominium owners to manage rental bookings for their units, while it also retains “the right to rent the dock slips” it owns in the resort’s marina. The judge also affirmed the rights of Old Bahama Bay’s 73 condo owners to “continue to access amenities” at Old Bahama Bay “subject to certain conditions”, which will help to shield them from any negative fall-out caused by the ongoing courtroom fight. And she has yet to rule on the substantive cases, featuring multiple claims and counter-claims, advanced by both LRA-OBB and IVRC. The legal battle between LRA-OBB and IVRC, which has now lasted for eight years, is part of a wider fight taking place on multiple fronts to determine West End’s future development. Separate and apart from the control issues now before Justice Delancy, the outcome of a near-$10m tax dispute will also play a key role in resolving the former Ginn project’s fate. For LRA-OBB and Resorts Holdings, the other owner of the former Ginn project’s real estate, are contesting the Department of Inland Revenue and Bahamas Treasurer’s bid to seize and sell-off one of the development’s 1,400-acre land parcels over near-$10m in allegedly unpaid real property taxes. A Tax Appeal Commission decision on this is expected imminently. It also urged the Supreme Court to prevent “obstruction of roadways, walkways, services and beach access.. to the units and exclusion from common property”, and direct an inspection of flooded units in building 15. Not surprisingly, this was resisted by LRA-OBB. articles.desc: Succession should preserve capable leadership and institutional knowledge instead of merely transferring ownership to a relative.
articles.content: Family Businesses Survive When Leaders Learn to Let Go | Opinion - Newsweek A family business can spend a century building trust and lose it in a single generation. Leaders quite often confuse ownership with responsibility. The company carries their name, their history, and perhaps four generations of family sacrifice, so they begin to believe its future should follow their wishes. Yet a business is a living institution, sustained by employees who give it their working lives, customers who trust its products, and suppliers who depend on its stability. Its owner may hold the shares, but the consequences of its decisions belong to a much wider community. This is why succession deserves far more attention than it receives. Deloitte’s 2026 global family business research found that 40 percent of family businesses expect a CEO change within the next decade, while only 46 percent have broad, well-developed succession plans. Those figures reveal a dangerous gap between knowing change is coming and preparing for it. Passing the business to a son, daughter, or another relative is a decision about ownership. Preparing someone to protect its people and future is a decision about leadership. I lead a family-owned automotive chemicals company with four generations of my family behind it. I also have a newborn son, and I would love to give him the opportunity to choose whether he wants to be part of the business someday. That choice matters to me because my responsibility is to leave him an opportunity, not an obligation. The company must be worth inheriting, whoever eventually leads it. My understanding of leadership has also been shaped by people outside my family. I have learned from leaders whose experience, judgment, and ability to bring people together have challenged my own assumptions. A surname cannot guarantee competence, just as a different surname cannot diminish it. The leader best equipped to take a company forward may be the person who has earned the trust of its people and understands its customers most deeply. What Is at Stake! What happens when a leader refuses to accept this? An unprepared successor can take control, experienced employees may leave, product standards slip, and customers will gradually take their loyalty elsewhere. The company may retain its name while losing the qualities that gave that name value. A healthier future is possible when outgoing leaders prepare capable successors, invest in their workforce, and give the next generation room to make necessary changes. One path leaves a company weakened by personal ambition; the other gives employees, customers, and communities a business they can continue to rely on. What people may fail to see is that a failed succession can threaten livelihoods, disrupt supply chains, and remove trusted products from people’s lives. A successful one, however, can preserve jobs, support local economies, and give future generations a place to build careers. Every consumer who depends on a reliable product, every employee who needs a stable income, and every small supplier awaiting payment has a stake in how a business changes hands. Selling to private equity can make financial sense for an owner who has spent decades building a valuable company. The offer may provide security for a family and a substantial return on years of work. Yet the purchase price is only one measure of what is being transferred. What happens to the people who know the business inside out? Will product quality remain a priority? Will customer relationships receive the same care once financial targets begin to dominate decisions? articles.title: PaperPilot runs locally. Your agent still has a data boundary.
articles.desc: A PDF can stay on your computer while information from it travels somewhere else. No contradiction required. The local tool and the agent using it occupy different parts of the system. 📄 PaperPilot is getting attention for a Rust document engine exposed through a CLI, browser interface, desktop app,
articles.content: A PDF can stay on your computer while information from it travels somewhere else. No contradiction required. The local tool and the agent using it occupy different parts of the system. 📄 PaperPilot is getting attention for a Rust document engine exposed through a CLI, browser interface, desktop app, local HTTP service and MCP server. The appealing part is straightforward: common document operations do not have to begin with uploading a PDF to a conversion website. [1] But when I connect a local tool to an assistant, I want to trace the return path, too. Where do the filenames, search queries, extracted text and error messages go after the tool finishes? Original source-traced architecture diagram. The provider arrow is conditional on the client's configuration; it is not a captured PaperPilot network trace. Follow a concrete operation through the source 🔎 At the pinned PaperPilot revision linked below, pdf_extract_text loads the input file, runs the extraction operation, joins the extracted pages and writes the result to the requested output path. Its successful operation result contains a success message and that output path. Its data field is empty. [2] That detail matters. It would be inaccurate to say this operation always sends the complete extracted document back in its MCP reply. In this branch, it writes the text to a file and reports where it went. Now add an agent. If the client subsequently reads that output file to summarize it, the extracted text may enter the client's model request. That is a separate action with a separate data flow. Whether it reaches a hosted provider depends on the client, model and surrounding configuration. The original PDF need never be uploaded for its contents to become part of a prompt. Equally, using MCP does not mean contents must be uploaded. A local model and local tool can keep that part of the path local. 💡 A tool result is information, too PaperPilot's pdf_search branch illustrates a different return shape. It searches a document and builds a message reporting matching page indices, or that no matches were found. The general response wrapper serializes the operation result into MCP text content. [2] That is much less than returning the whole document. It can still disclose a fact about it: whether a particular query matched, and where. A file path can also reveal a client name or a project label before anyone reads a page. I think of this as a set of envelopes rather than a single “local/cloud” switch: The input envelope: file bytes and paths made available to the process. The result envelope: messages, metadata, paths or content returned to the client. The model envelope: whatever that client actually places in a subsequent model request. The envelopes can overlap. Inspecting one does not tell you everything about the others. Choose the surface for the job For a deterministic merge or rotation, a local CLI can avoid involving a model at all. That removes the model-request envelope from that particular workflow. For interactive document work, a browser or desktop surface may be more convenient. For language-driven orchestration, MCP gives the agent a tool interface. None of those choices alone establishes the complete privacy story. A browser-delivered application still needs its own review; a local service needs an appropriate binding and access policy; an agent needs a decision about what it may read and send. These are different questions, even when the underlying PDF operation is shared. ⚠️ A common mistake is to treat “stdio” as a confidentiality certificate. It describes how processes exchange messages. It does not describe what a client does with those messages afterward. MCP roots provide a way for clients to describe intended filesystem boundaries, and the specification asks servers to validate paths against them. A declared root is not, by itself, proof that an operating system prevents a process from reading anything else. [3] The inspection I would actually perform I would start with a synthetic document containing a distinctive harmless phrase. Inspect the tool request, tool response and any subsequent file read separately. Then inspect what the configured client sends to its model. Keep logs themselves inside the intended boundary. That sequence gives specific answers: did a path leave, did content leave, and which component sent it? It is more informative than watching the document tool alone and declaring the entire agent session offline. ✅ This article is a source-based architecture explanation. I have not run PaperPilot's PDF engine, captured its network traffic or audited every operation or dependency. The conditional flows above are an interpretation of the inspected branches and the client/tool boundary, not a security certification or an allegation of observed leakage. Local document processing is a useful capability. I just want the word “local” attached to the component it actually describes. References [1] PaperPilot, project overview. [2] PaperPilot, MCP operation handlers at revision ba6c05d, especially pdf_extract_text, pdf_search and the operation-result wrapper. The setup guide distinguishes the server from each agent's model authentication. [3] Model Context Protocol, roots and path-validation guidance. Original architecture diagram created for this article. No third-party project imagery reused. AI disclosure AI was used to draft the article.

Homemade soda bubbles up as a new kitchen trend With searches for homemade soda soaring, a new generation of home brewers are experimenting with fruit, fermentation and ginger bugs to make their own fizz. Move over kombucha, homemade soda is bubbling up as the latest kitchen experiment. In India, searches for “homemade soda” on Google have risen by more than 5,000% over the past month, while global interest has climbed 130%. On social media, reels on #homemadesoda and #fermentedsoda are pulling in millions of views, as people experiment with fruit, ginger bugs and fermentation. For some, it is a way to cut back on packaged soft drinks. For others, it is an analogue hobby to tinker with at home. Sahana Acharya, 28, started making homemade soda to reduce her dependency on soft drinks. The internet offered an unlikely solution. “I found a reel where the creator was making pineapple tepache (a lightly fermented Mexican drink made from pineapple rinds), and I was intrigued,” she says. Her first attempt worked, leaving her hooked on flavours, from jackfruit and mangosteen to rambutan and pineapple. articles.desc: On Oct 22, I read the word "Merged" twice. It was my first contribution to Forem (the platform that hosts dev.to). I don't write Ruby. A coding assistant wrote the code, and it still took 12 weeks. To explain why that word mattered, I have to start in 2019. I kinda discovered dev.to in around April
articles.content: On Oct 22, I read the word "Merged" twice. It was my first contribution to Forem (the platform that hosts dev.to). I don't write Ruby. A coding assistant wrote the code, and it still took 12 weeks. To explain why that word mattered, I have to start in 2019. I kinda discovered dev.to in around April 2019 and at the time I didn't really get into it. It was just one of the many resources I'd search when I wanted to find solutions to bugs or to create features. One time or two it'd show up in my Google search and then I'd click off it. In April 2021 I finally signed up for an account on dev.to. I heard being social is an important aspect to make in this industry. I knew at the time blogging was the easiest for me. I'd never really built a network in the industry, I'd just started following people on LinkedIn and Twitter and my projects were all unknown. I wasn't really the kind of person who'd self-promote and ask for a job. It just wasn't right for me. I'm also an introvert. I wasn't really comfortable meeting new people and I was also very conscious of what they think of me. The Nigerian dev communities didn't help either. They were just hostile to newbies like me. I didn't even have a mentor or friend to learn with. I only ever used the platform to read articles, and I never took the time to write any posts or comments. I didn't even remember my account existed. In November 2025, I created another account to boost my online visibility. I'd noticed that searching my name in Google only resulted in my LinkedIn and Facebook profiles. So here I am, with 62,275 followers and 109 posts. dev.to is the second most used app on my phone (after X), and I refresh it frequently. dev.to is how I met developers outside Nigeria. I had been wanting to dig into Forem for months, but because Forem is built on Rails, and I don't write Ruby, I held off. However, when DEV announced the Summer Bug Smash, and Jess Lee's post came out, that was the final push I needed. The bug fix was small. It took 12 weeks to merge, most of it waiting. Here is how it went. Looking at the code was not the easiest thing to do. I could not tell which issues I could or couldn't fix, so I used an AI coding assistant to help me figure it out. Back in July, the repo had 34 open issues. Some of them were not actually bugs. One was a question the maintainers had already answered. One was an account problem that went to support. And none of the issues were labeled "good first issue". So I chose #23687, which was a small bug: the Posts count on the dashboard was different than the Posts tab. Since the issue description was short, I could follow it. The coding assistant identified the issue and told me how to fix it: the badge was including the count of statuses and archived posts, while the tab was not. The coding assistant wrote the code fix and the tests, and explained what was going on. I recognized it as a typical JavaScript issue: the count didn't match the list after filtering. Here is the fix that was merged. First, the sidebar action sets the count: def sidebar @user = current_user @organizations = @user.admin_organizations @action = params[:state] + @posts_count = posts_count_for(@user) end Then a helper counts the same posts the tab lists: # The "Posts" nav item always links to the default (non-archived, full posts # only) view of the user's own dashboard, so its indicator should reflect # that same scope rather than the user's raw articles_count, which also # includes statuses and archived posts that never show up in that list. def posts_count_for(user) And the badge reads that number, not articles_count: - + The mobile menu got the same one-line change. The rest of the PR is the test. Since I did not have Ruby installed on my machine, I couldn't run the tests. I created a PR and let the Forem CI run the tests. I was a bit weirded out that I submitted a PR to code I couldn't read line by line. The CI failed the first time, but the issue was in the test, not the code. The GitHub status also showed "Merging is blocked", and I assumed a maintainer would have to merge it. That was correct. I then signed the CLA, and waited. After a while, I forgot about it, until I got a notification. Then a reviewer approved the PR on Oct 20 and noticed I had added a line I should not have. So I asked the maintainers if they wanted me to remove it, and two days later Mikey (a maintainer) removed it and merged. First, I felt relieved, then proud. That evening, DEV sent me the DEV Contributor badge. It was sent to my old account. I remembered about my old account because of the badge email. Small fixes are still fixes, and now, someone using the dashboard will see the correct post count. I entered the fix in the Summer Bug Smash on Aug 3 while it was still awaiting review. And about 11 weeks later, it got merged. I did not win the Bug Smash, but this counts as a win to me. I learned most of what I know about software development from reading open source projects: the code, documentation, and GitHub issues. This is my first contribution to Forem, and nobody asked me where I was from or what my job title was. They just reviewed my change. That is part of why I love open source. Forem was special, because it was an open source project powering a site I used on a daily basis. The AI coding assistant transformed my side of things. It helped me submit a fix that got merged by a maintainer. And AI changed the other side of things as well. The Forem README welcomes AI-assisted pull requests, and will reject "slop". The repo has an AGENTS.md that outlines how coding assistants should work. The review on my PR says it was written by an AI agent, and the line I should not have added passed the CI. It only got caught by the reviewer. Both sides now have AI, but it is ultimately up to a human to make a decision. That's where the trust comes in. People still question the utility of AI. After the line that slipped past CI, I understand why. I still could not have sent this fix without it. AI might take the ability to write code out of the equation entirely. For example, I know when building an API, I need to spin up a server, create a router, set up route paths to point to handlers, serialize and deserialize the body. When learning a new language, I am trying to figure out how to accomplish these tasks, rather than trying to understand what needs to be accomplished. Removing this limitation also means I can develop with the language more appropriate for the system. AI could change the mindset about hiring, from devs who understand their language to devs who understand systems. If you want to contribute to Forem: Don't wait for a "good first issue". There were none available in July. Any issue labeled "bug" and "always open for contribution" is up for grabs. Verify the issue is a real bug. Some were not. Check if the issue has an assignee. Some were already taken. Sign the CLA. That's one comment on your PR. Add a test. The README says all PRs should include tests. If you're unable to run the tests locally, state it in your PR, and let CI run the tests. I did, and the failing tests in my first run turned out to be a good thing. Be patient. My PR took 12 weeks. Special thanks to Jess for posting about the Bug Smash, and for encouraging me to finally dig into the repo; Ben for creating DEV and Forem; Mikey for reviewing my PR, pushing the cleanup, and merging it; and everyone who answered my comments. Fix dashboard "Posts" count to match what the Posts tab shows #23690 dannwaneri posted on Jul 30, 2026 Fixes the count mismatch described in #23687. Problem The "Posts" indicator in the dashboard sidebar (_actions.html.erb / _actions_mobile.html.erb) renders @user.articles_count, which is a counter_culture cache on User that counts every Article row belonging to the user, regardless of type_of (full_post, status, fullscreen_embed) or archived state. But the "Posts" nav link always opens the default dashboard view (DashboardsController#show with no params), which only lists non-archived, full_post-type articles — statuses and archived posts are filtered out. So any user who has ever posted a status/boost update or archived a post sees a "Posts" badge that's higher than the number of posts actually listed under that tab, matching the report in #23687 ("Posts 2" shown after publishing only 1 post). Fix Add a posts_count_for(user) helper in DashboardsController that counts articles with the same scope as what's actually displayed (full_posts, archived: false, from_subforem), and use it via a new @posts_count ivar in both the full-page render (#show) and the AJAX sidebar partial (#sidebar) instead of the raw counter cache. User#articles_count itself is left untouched since it's used elsewhere (badges, spam heuristics, etc.) where the broader "all articles ever" semantics are correct. Testing Added regression specs in spec/requests/dashboard_spec.rb covering both the #show and #sidebar actions: a user with one full post, one status, and one archived post should see posts_count of 1. Note: I wasn't able to run the Rails test suite locally (no Ruby/Postgres environment on this machine), so I'm relying on CI to confirm the specs pass — flagging that openly in case a maintainer wants to double check before merging. Four separate CVEs in one release, all stack overwrites, all in zone-file parsing, all fixed in 4.15.3. The common thread is a parser t
articles.content: Four overflow bugs, one coding lesson: what NSD 4.15.3 says about parser hardening Reading the NSD advisories side by side produces a lesson broader than the patch. Four separate CVEs in one release, all stack overwrites, all in zone-file parsing, all fixed in 4.15.3. The common thread is a parser that trusted a derived length. Any team maintaining software that consumes semi-trusted structured input can learn from the specific ways that trust failed. The pattern in the four CVEs CVE-2026-101341 is the clearest illustration. Text tokens shorter than 32 bytes were not checked against the space reserved for RDATA, so an arbitrarily sized out-of-bounds write became possible, and the advisory notes it can cover a callback function pointer used right after parsing. CVE-2026-101337 is arithmetic drift. Base64 data split into pieces of three characters or less had token sizes computed as zero bytes, so the parser believed it needed no room while the decoder wrote up to 64 KB. CVE-2026-101339 is a boundary that held for the record but not for the field appended to it. A HIP record filled near or at its RDATA limit, plus a rendezvous server, wrote 191 bytes past the stack buffer. CVE-2026-101338 is an unbounded decode after a failed limit check. A SVCB or HTTPS record filled to the brim, an extra ECH parameter, and the base64 decoder writes data of unrestricted size. Three properties that would have prevented all four First, a single length authority. In each case the parser had two notions of size: the space reserved and the length derived from input. When code has one variable that both the allocation and the write consult, the disagreement disappears. Second, bounded decoders. The base64 path in CVE-2026-101338 and CVE-2026-101337 wrote based on its own view of the data. A decoder that takes an explicit destination capacity turns an unbounded write into a rejection. Third, checked pointer arithmetic before callback use. CVE-2026-101341 reached a callback function pointer because the overflow was not confined to a buffer that the parser merely read from. Placing callbacks and function tables outside writable parser memory reduces the value of a nearby overflow. Why zone files deserve hostile-input treatment Zone files look like configuration. Operators edit them by hand, scripts generate them, control panels render them. That appearance encourages parsers to treat the content as trusted. The advisories are explicit that files NSD writes itself avoid the problematic shapes, which is exactly the assumption that breaks when another system produces the file. The same reasoning applies beyond DNS. Certificate signing requests, routing policy imports, mail filter rules, and package metadata all arrive as structured text that another program generated. Every one of those parsers has the same structural risk. Testing that finds these bugs Fuzzing remains the practical method. A harness that feeds structured records into the parser and varies lengths at field boundaries would reach CVE-2026-101341 and CVE-2026-101337 quickly, because both are length accounting errors near small thresholds. CVE-2026-101339 needs the harness to append a second field to a record already at its limit, and CVE-2026-101338 needs the harness to respect wire-format sizing so the overflow requires a plausible record rather than random bytes. One addition to a fuzzing pipeline pays off here: assert on the invariant after every parse. If the parser exposes a count of bytes written, compare it against the bytes reserved and fail the test when they diverge. That turns a memory-safety bug into a clear assertion failure. Affected scope and remediation NSD 4.10.0 through 4.15.2 inclusive; earlier releases and 4.15.3 are not affected. SecurityOnline reports a CVSS v4 score of 8.7 for each CVE with no public exploit at publication. Upgrade to NSD 4.15.3 from https://nlnetlabs.nl/downloads/nsd/nsd-4.15.3.tar.gz. Backports can use the published diffs, for example https://nlnetlabs.nl/downloads/nsd/patch_CVE-2026-101338.diff, applied with patch -p1 then make install. Verify the running binary afterwards, and use the fixed nsd-checkzone to review production zones. No count indicates version or configuration. articles.desc: Astronomers use JWST to map ancient supermassive black hole hidden by cosmic dust
articles.content: Astronomers use JWST to map ancient supermassive black hole Astronomers use JWST to map ancient supermassive black hole hidden by cosmic dust Astronomers have found a huge, dust-reddened quasar that existed less than a billion years after the Big Bang. Daming Yang and his team at Leiden Observatory shared their findings about J1440+0019 in a recent paper on the arXiv preprint server. This quasar is at a redshift of 6.55 and contains a supermassive black hole that is quickly growing and weighs about 1.1 billion times the mass of our Sun. Scientists are especially interested in quasars from this time in the universe. This era matches the period of cosmic reionization, when ultraviolet light from the first stars and galaxies removed electrons from neutral hydrogen gas throughout the universe. Usually, scientists search for early active galactic nuclei by looking for bright ultraviolet light. But this approach often does not work for systems covered in thick dust, since the dust blocks the UV light. As a result, only a few of these hidden, reddened quasars have been found at high redshifts. To see through the dust around J1440+0019, the team used near-infrared spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope along with cold gas data from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. The spectral data showed that the object is a red type-1 quasar. Astronomers can see its galactic center directly, but the view is still blocked by a lot of dust. The team also saw strong blueshifted absorption systems moving as fast as 3,600 kilometers per second. These speeds suggest there are powerful outflows pushing material away from the center. Further analysis found that the supermassive black hole is eating matter very quickly and is shining at about 80 percent of its theoretical Eddington limit. The galaxy around it is also very extreme. The galaxy has about 400 million times the Sun’s mass in dust and is one of the brightest sources of ionized carbon emission at this distance. Scientists estimate it could be forming up to 1,330 new stars each year. The team pointed out that ALMA collected the needed dust tracers in only five and a half minutes. This shows that future quick surveys could find similar targets for more detailed study without using too much telescope time. Upcoming missions such as the Roman Space Telescope will probably help close the current gap in observations and create a more complete list of these hidden cosmic giants. articles.content: New CoPAIR program connects Cornell researchers with AI tools, training and community | The National Tribune As AI tools become increasingly influential in academia, Cornell researchers need ways to evaluate what these tools can do, understand their limitations and develop reliable approaches for applying them thoughtfully, effectively, and responsibly. Communities of Practice for AI-enabled Research (OVPR), gives researchers access to emerging AI tools, hands-on training and collaborative communities where they can share best practices, develop disciplinary norms for appropriate AI use and non-use, and evaluate new tools for research. The program is designed for researchers at any stage of AI experience, from those exploring it for the first time to those already building it into their workflows. By bringing domain experts around common AI challenges and opportunities and connecting them with tools, training, and collaborative support, the CoPAIR program reflects Cornell’s commitment to enabling a community-driven approach to responsible AI use. “Every researcher and every research field are somewhere different on their AI journey, facing their own AI frontiers, crises, and unknowns,” said , associate vice provost for research and lead of the research pillar for the Cornell AI Initiative. “As we confront them, we need open platforms for research communities to come together to collectively shape the path forward. The CoPAIR program offers one such platform to critically examine our shared research commitments and standards, learn new techniques and tools, and advance scientific methods and reproducible workflows.” CoPAIR is built on two pillars: Research Pod CoPAIR and Core-Center CoPAIR. Research Pod CoPAIR: researchers learning together are small, self-formed groups of domain-based researchers who come together to explore questions and practices around AI use in their shared field. Guided by Cornell’s coordinated “AI in the disciplines” framework, each pod is a collaborative space to test relevant tools and methods, explore where and how AI can be used effectively, and build practical knowledge. “AI brings opportunities and challenges to nearly every discipline,” said , vice provost for AI strategy. “Meeting the moment depends on researchers who understand AI in relation to the practices of their fields. CoPAIR gives them the space, the support and a collaborative platform to develop norms and best practices for their scholarship.” Core-Center CoPAIR: shared hubs for AI expertise In the second pillar, Core-Center CoPAIRs are research communities anchored within existing Cornell centers, institutes, and shared research infrastructure. Building on their established networks for collaboration and community building, Core-Center CoPAIRs serve as AI research hubs that offer domain-specific AI expertise, training, and resource sharing. The first Core-Center CoPAIR pilot is led by the (BRC), a hub for Cornell’s biotechnology and life sciences community. The approximately eight-week fall 2026 pilot focuses on four areas of life sciences research: genomics, including transcriptomics, epigenomics and metagenomics; proteomics and metabolomics; imaging; and structural biology. While the pillars differ in structure, both are designed to develop norms and best practices for AI-enabled research and share what they learn with the broader Cornell research community. Through experimentation, collaboration, and evaluation of emerging tools, CoPAIRs develop and disseminate practical guidance, use cases, templates, and best practices for the responsible use and non-use of AI. They also curate shared repositories of AI agent skills and research applications and help researchers integrate general-purpose and specialized AI for Science tools into their work. Researchers interested in forming a Research Pod CoPAIR or joining the Core-Center CoPAIR pilot can learn more and apply at the Cornell AI Initiative website /Public Release. View in full The

articles.desc: A massive new simulation reconstructs the early universe, offering astronomers a powerful way to investigate the birth of galaxies and the transformation of cosmic matter.
articles.content: Scientists Just Recreated the First 2 Billion Years of the Universe on a Staggering Scale Scientists have reconstructed the universe’s first 2 billion years in one of the largest and most detailed cosmic simulations ever developed. Called , the model follows the formation of early galaxies and the transformation of hydrogen and helium across an enormous region of space. The research, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society , gives astronomers a new way to test whether their theories can explain the distant galaxies being observed by the A Virtual Universe Larger Than Anything Previously Modeled at This Detail Reconstructing the early universe presents a challenge that goes far beyond calculating where the first galaxies formed. Scientists must also account for the gravitational pull of , the movement and heating of ordinary gas, and the radiation released as the earliest luminous objects emerged. Each of these processes influences the others, creating a complex physical system that must be followed as the universe expands. Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian developed Lumina to bring these interactions together on an unusually large scale. The simulation belongs to a class known as cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics models , which combine the behavior of matter with the transport of radiation through space. This allows researchers to study not only the growth of cosmic structures but also how the light produced by those structures changes their surroundings. Lumina represents a volume of space equivalent to a cube measuring approximately than those used in previous comparable calculations. This expanded coverage gives scientists the ability to examine cosmic environments that smaller simulations cannot represent as fully, while retaining enough detail to investigate the galaxies responsible for changing those environments. Scale matters because the early universe was not a uniform collection of galaxies evolving in isolation. Dense regions attracted matter and developed luminous structures, while less populated areas remained comparatively dark. Radiation from emerging galaxies traveled through the surrounding gas, gradually altering conditions far beyond the galaxies themselves. A simulation restricted to a small region may reproduce individual objects in considerable detail but miss the broader cosmic environment shaping their evolution. Lumina is designed to bridge that gap, connecting the development of galaxies to changes occurring across vast distances. The result is a model that can be compared with astronomical surveys covering enormous regions of the distant universe, rather than serving only as a detailed reconstruction of relatively small cosmic neighborhoods. The research, was Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society How the First Galaxies Transformed the Gas Between Them One of Lumina’s central scientific objectives is to reconstruct , a period when radiation from early luminous objects changed the electrical state of gas spread throughout the universe. After the universe cooled enough for electrons to combine with atomic nuclei, much of its hydrogen existed as neutral atoms. As the earliest stars and galaxies formed, their energetic radiation began stripping electrons from those atoms, producing ionized hydrogen. Over time, expanding ionized regions spread through intergalactic space and reshaped the physical conditions in which subsequent generations of galaxies developed. Helium underwent its own ionization history. Because removing electrons from helium requires different amounts of energy, its evolution provides additional information about the radiation sources present during early cosmic history.
